summary: Describes Extreme Networks' Ethernet Automatic Protection Switching (EAPS), a technology invented by that company to make Ethernet rings more available and robust. An EAPS ring can be resilient in a way comparable to SONET rings, at lower cost and with fewer limits such as ring size. It is a vendor description, published as informational.

eli5.summary: Kids in a circle pass a ball. If one kid steps out, the ball goes the other way around the circle. This describes a company's trick for keeping network rings working when one link breaks.

questions: how does ethernet ring protection work
what is the difference between eaps and sonet rings
subtitle: Fast protection switching for Ethernet networks arranged in rings.

tldr.problem: Networks arranged in ring topology are vulnerable to a single fiber cut or link failure that breaks the loop. SONET rings provide resilience but are expensive and have constraints like maximum ring size.
tldr.mechanism: Extreme Networks' Ethernet Automatic Protection Switching (EAPS) uses a master node that blocks one port in normal operation, preventing loops. When it detects a link failure, the master unblocks that port to allow traffic around the break. The system converges in less than one second, often under 50 milliseconds.
tldr.outcome: EAPS provides SONET-like resilience for Ethernet rings at lower cost and without ring-size constraints. It works on standard Ethernet switches and can run multiple independent domains on the same ring.

facts.label: Convergence time
facts.value: Less than 1 second, typically under 50 milliseconds

today: RFC 3619 is an Informational RFC describing Extreme Networks' proprietary EAPS technology. While not a standards-track protocol, it documents a practical vendor solution to Ethernet ring protection that has been deployed in metropolitan area networks. The technology remains relevant for specific Ethernet ring deployments.

sections.title: Introduction to Ethernet Rings
sections.content:
Many Metropolitan Area Networks (MANs) and some Local Area Networks (LANs) have a ring topology, where fiber optic cables form a circle of nodes. In normal operation, a ring provides two paths between any two points. However, standard Ethernet assumes there are no loops (via the Spanning Tree Protocol), creating a conflict with ring topology.

SONET rings are expensive solutions that provide protection switching, but require special equipment and have constraints such as maximum ring sizes. Extreme Networks developed Ethernet Automatic Protection Switching (EAPS) to provide similar resilience on standard Ethernet rings. EAPS converges in less than one second when detecting link failures, often in less than 50 milliseconds. Convergence time is independent of the number of nodes in the ring.
sections.eli5: Network rings are useful for reliability, but regular Ethernet does not expect loops. A company invented a clever trick to make Ethernet rings work reliably when a cable breaks.

sections.title: Master and Transit Nodes
sections.content:
In an EAPS Domain on a single Ethernet ring, there is one designated master node and all other nodes are transit nodes. Each node on the ring has two ports connected to the ring. The master node designates one as the primary port and the other as the secondary port.

In normal operation, the master node blocks its secondary port for all non-control frames belonging to the EAPS Domain. This makes the ring appear to have no loop from Ethernet's perspective, allowing standard switching and learning to work correctly. A special Control VLAN can always pass through all ports, even the blocked secondary port. When the master node detects a ring fault, it unblocks its secondary port to allow data frames to flow around the break.
sections.eli5: One special switch holds the ring closed by blocking one of its two connections. The other switches just pass data through. When a cable breaks, the special switch opens that blocked connection to let traffic go the other way.

sections.title: Link Detection and Recovery
sections.content:
EAPS uses two mechanisms to detect failures. The Link Down Alert mechanism allows any transit node that detects a link-down condition to immediately send a control frame on the Control VLAN to the master node. When the master receives this alert, it transitions to ring-fault state and unblocks its secondary port. It also flushes its bridging table and sends a flush command to all other nodes.

The Ring Polling mechanism is a backup: the master node sends health-check frames at a configurable interval. If the ring is complete, the frame returns on the secondary port. If the master does not receive the frame before a fail-period timer expires, it enters ring-fault state and unblocks the secondary port. When the ring is restored, the master returns to normal state by re-blocking the secondary port and flushing its bridge table.
sections.eli5: The special switch checks regularly if the ring is intact by sending a test message around it. If the cable breaks, the message does not come back, so the switch opens its blocked port. When the cable is fixed, the switch closes the port again.

sections.title: Multiple Domains and Scalability
sections.content:
An EAPS-enabled switch can be part of multiple rings and thus belong to multiple EAPS Domains simultaneously. Each EAPS Domain on a switch requires a separate instance of the EAPS protocol, one instance per protected ring. Multiple independent EAPS domains can also run on the same ring at the same time, each with its own unique master node and set of protected VLANs.

This flexibility allows spatial reuse of the ring's bandwidth and support for different protection schemes for different traffic classes. The convergence time remains independent of the number of nodes in the ring, so EAPS scales well to larger rings without performance degradation. Any Ethernet VLAN that needs protection is configured on all ports in the ring for the EAPS Domain.
sections.eli5: A switch can be part of many rings and protect different groups of computers on each ring using the same mechanism. Adding more switches to the ring does not slow down the failure detection.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Anyone with physical access to the physical layer connections could forge any Ethernet frame, including EAPS control frames. Such forgeries could be used to disrupt an Ethernet network by triggering false link-down alerts or corrupting state information.

The RFC recommends that users not deploy Ethernet in environments where active physical-layer attacks are considered a significant risk without some form of link-layer encryption. IEEE standards for link-layer encryption already exist and could protect Ethernet links. Alternatively, upper-layer security mechanisms could be used if they better suit the local threat model. The security considerations are the same as for any other Ethernet bridge mechanism.
sections.eli5: If someone can physically touch the network cables, they could fool the system. Encryption at the link level can prevent this from breaking your network.
